attribute_05.text:
Proposed approach

• Kickoff and discovery (Week 1): confirm scope, source-handling rules, interview roster, evidence requests, and the working schedule.
• Interviews and artifact review (Weeks 2–4): engage ESS, RIS, and IAM leadership and practitioners; review authorized SDLC, security, deployment/operations, monitoring, incident, and AI-readiness evidence.
• Analysis and synthesis (Weeks 4–5): assess each group across software development, security, deployment/operations, and AI readiness; separate evidence confidence from maturity; identify cross-cutting strengths, gaps, and dependencies.
• Draft report and review (Weeks 6–7): provide traceable findings and phased practice/process recommendations for sponsor review, preserving unresolved evidence gaps rather than filling them with assumptions.
• Final report (Week 7–8): reconcile supported feedback, retain limitations and evidence provenance, and deliver the final written package.

Methodology

The assessment is evidence-led and practitioner-centered. Interviews establish context but do not automatically prove implementation. Findings are traced to observed evidence, scoped to the service/team population actually reviewed, and labeled for confidence, recency, representativeness, and corroboration. Materially conflicting evidence remains unresolved until bounded or reconciled. Recommendations are prioritized by expected impact and implementation complexity, phased into near-, medium-, and longer-term actions, and kept at the practice/process level rather than individual performance or specific commercial product/vendor selection.

Interview plan

For each participating group, use the University’s proposed mix of leadership, managers, and individual contributors. Begin with workflow and responsibility mapping, then use concrete examples and artifacts to test stated practice. Cross-group synthesis occurs only after per-group evidence is established. The integrated schedule targets the University’s six-to-eight-week window; exact interview times, onsite sessions, and kickoff date remain subject to contracting and University/prime coordination.

attribute_09.text:
The proposed engagement is a fixed-scope, evidence-led assessment of Enterprise Student Systems (ESS), Research Information Systems (RIS), and Identity & Access Management (IAM) across software development, security, deployment/operations, and AI readiness.

Approach and framework: use structured interviews plus authorized artifacts to build a traceable evidence register; assess each group independently before cross-cutting synthesis; distinguish maturity from confidence in the supporting evidence; preserve missing, stale, or conflicting evidence as explicit limitations; and produce prioritized, phased practice/process recommendations. The assessment excludes line-by-line code review, formal compliance audit, individual performance evaluation, and recommendations for specific commercial products/vendors.

Schedule: target seven to eight weeks from kickoff: Week 1 kickoff/discovery; Weeks 2–4 interviews/artifact review; Weeks 4–5 analysis/synthesis; Weeks 6–7 draft/review; Week 7–8 final delivery. Exact kickoff, interview, and onsite dates remain subject to contracting and University coordination.

Deliverables: executive-ready written report; documented methodology/peer context; per-group findings; cross-cutting themes; prioritized short-, medium-, and longer-horizon roadmap actions; evidence/limitations register; and reproducibility/currentness material for the technical assessment artifacts.

Commercial preparation state: the current TJLabs technical workshare proposes $24,000 fixed for its bounded base production workshare, with optional final-readout support at $4,000 only if separately authorized. This is not yet a submission-ready total Supplier price: the RFQ requires Supplier pricing inclusive of expected expenses, while the current TJLabs workshare expressly excludes travel. The authorized bidder must reconcile integrated staffing, references, travel/expense treatment, and total Supplier pricing before this field or [[ATTACH:proposal]] is finalized.

Team and references: names, roles, qualifications, bidder-level references, and final responsibility allocation remain authorized-bidder inputs and must be inserted from verified source material before submission.

attribute_12.text:
Stakeholder involvement will be structured so evidence collection, interpretation, and recommendation development remain transparent to the people who operate and govern the assessed services.

At kickoff, confirm the engagement sponsor, day-to-day University contact, ESS/RIS/IAM group leads, evidence custodians, and the interview roster. For each group, interview a mix of leadership, managers, and individual contributors representing different roles in the delivery lifecycle. Use leadership interviews to establish objectives, governance, and decision context; practitioner interviews and artifacts to test how work is actually performed; and group-lead checkpoints to resolve scope or evidence gaps.

During analysis, distinguish group-specific findings from department-level themes rather than forcing different stacks into one operating model. Materially concerning findings should be surfaced privately to the day-to-day contact and sponsor before publication, while the final assessment remains transparent to participating groups. Draft recommendations should be reviewed for factual accuracy, dependencies, adoption burden, and implementation practicality without allowing unsupported feedback to erase evidence-backed limitations.

Recommended informed/involved groups are the CIO/engagement sponsor, AIS day-to-day contact, ESS/RIS/IAM leadership, representative software/security/operations practitioners, relevant policy or data owners when an issue crosses domains, and any University stakeholders responsible for implementing accepted roadmap actions. The rationale is to combine executive context with direct workflow evidence and implementation ownership.

attribute_13.text:
Issues that warrant explicit attention in addition to the named assessment domains include:

• Evidence quality and comparability: distinguish stated policy from demonstrated practice, record source recency and scope, and avoid generalizing a single service or team sample.
• Cross-group consistency versus healthy variation: determine where ESS, RIS, and IAM need common guardrails and where different stacks or operating contexts justify different implementation patterns.
• Recovery evidence: separate successful backup jobs from demonstrated restoration, dependency recovery, and verified business-function recovery; where objectives are supplied, compare observed restoration evidence to the stated RPO/RTO.
• Delivery measurement quality: establish service-scoped definitions and denominators before interpreting lead time, deployment frequency, failed-deployment recovery time, change fail rate, or deployment rework rate.
• Test-data and sensitive-data handling: examine whether non-production workflows minimize exposure while preserving useful test coverage.
• Decision traceability: ensure recommendations can be traced to evidence and limitations, especially for security and AI-readiness topics where policy, tooling, and actual practice can diverge.
• Adoption capacity: prioritize recommendations with explicit implementation effort, ownership, dependencies, and practitioner impact so the roadmap is realistic for a multi-application central IT organization.

These are proposed assessment lenses, not pre-judged University findings.

attribute_14.text:
Inherent project risks and planned controls include:

• Incomplete or uneven evidence across ESS, RIS, and IAM. Control: maintain an explicit evidence-request and gap register; use HOLD/unknown states instead of inferring maturity from missing material.
• Interview bias or self-reported practice being treated as proof. Control: corroborate material findings with artifacts or bounded examples and label evidence confidence.
• Comparing unlike teams or services. Control: assess service/group context first, define common measurement semantics, and only then synthesize cross-cutting themes.
• Scope drift into audit, individual performance evaluation, deep code review, or product/vendor selection. Control: preserve the RFQ scope boundary in interview plans, findings, and recommendation review.
• Sensitive information exposure. Control: use minimum-necessary evidence, authorized custody, no public-repository customer evidence, and the required confidentiality/destruction processes.
• Schedule compression or unavailable stakeholders. Control: identify critical interviews/artifacts early, surface blocked dependencies promptly, and keep the integrated six-to-eight-week schedule owned by the authorized engagement lead.
• Recommendations that are technically attractive but impractical to adopt. Control: phase actions by impact/complexity, identify skills/tooling/training dependencies, and review adoption burden with practitioners.
• Late source/amendment changes. Control: freeze source versions, track requirement deltas, and re-check the controlling eBid/RFQ materials before submission and before material assessment commitments.
